name: Autotuner
tagline: Hardware tool plus software suite for reading, writing and calibrating vehicle ECUs, licensed by credits.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is the thin part. The actual product is a physical flashing interface plus years of reverse engineered knowledge about how hundreds of ECU families authenticate, unlock, checksum and accept a write, sold as per vehicle credits. An agent can give you a very nice local bin inspector, map visualizer and datalog analyzer in an afternoon, and that is genuinely useful if you already own your dumps. It cannot give you working bench and OBD protocol support for a specific ECU, and the obvious shortcut of defeating the credit check is both illegal in most places and a good way to brick a car. Build the analysis half, pay for the flashing half, or do not touch it.
coreLoopDIY: Loads ECU binaries and CSV datalogs you already own, renders and diffs calibration maps against a definition file, and verifies checksums for documented formats, read only, no vehicle communication.
requirements: Your own legally obtained ECU dumps and datalogs
An XDF or A2L definition file if you want maps named instead of raw offsets
A real flashing tool, because this build never writes to a car
whatYouLose: Any ability to read from or write to an actual ECU
Protocol support for bench, boot and OBD modes across hundreds of ECU variants
Checksum correction for undocumented or encrypted calibration formats
Vendor support and the implied insurance when a flash goes wrong
Driver updates as manufacturers change security on new model years
moatNotes: The credit system is a billing wrapper around the real asset: a per ECU database of unlock sequences, memory layouts and checksum routines that took a long time and many bricked modules to assemble.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative to a supported tool is a dead immobiliser and a tow truck. Tuners are not paying for a pretty interface, they are paying for the specific certainty that this device, on this ECU, in this mode, will read and write without corrupting the flash, and for someone to call when it does not. Credits are annoying and the pricing is openly resented, but the cost of being wrong once exceeds a year of credits.
notes: A bin viewer is a weekend; talking to an ECU is not. The moat is the hardware plus a per vehicle library of unlock and checksum routines that nobody reconstructs from a prompt.
prompt:
Build a local, offline ECU calibration workbench. Python 3.11, Streamlit for the UI, numpy and pandas for data, no cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

In scope:
1. Load a raw ECU binary from disk (any size, treat as bytes). Show size, SHA256, and a hex view with jump-to-offset.
2. Load an XDF or A2L definition file if present and parse the table definitions it can handle: name, offset, rows, cols, data type, scaling equation, axis references. If parsing fails for an entry, skip it and list it under 'unparsed' instead of crashing.
3. Render any defined table as an editable grid plus a 3D surface and a heatmap. Apply the scaling equation for display, keep raw bytes as the source of truth.
4. Diff mode: load two binaries, list every defined table whose bytes differ, and show a cell level delta grid with changed cells highlighted.
5. Manual table mode for when there is no definition: user supplies offset, rows, cols, endianness and type, and the app renders it. Let them save that guess as a local JSON definition.
6. Datalog mode: load a CSV of logged channels, let the user map two columns to the axes of a chosen table and one to a value, then overlay a scatter of visited cells on the table heatmap with per cell mean and sample count.
7. Export: write modified bytes back to a NEW file only, never in place, and print a warning that no checksum has been corrected.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: any vehicle or OBD communication, any serial or CAN transport, any ECU unlock, seed-key or security access logic, any license, token or credit handling, any checksum algorithm that is not publicly documented, and any network calls at all.

Ship: app.py, a definitions/ folder, a parsers/ package with xdf.py and a2l.py, pytest tests using a synthetic 512KB binary and a hand written definition fixture, a requirements.txt, and a README that states plainly that this tool reads and edits files and cannot flash a car.
Store nothing outside the working directory. No .env is needed because there are no secrets.
